Main.sentence: Sarah Louise Palin ( ___E:PAY-lin U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Pronunciation_respelling_key)___ ; née Heath ; born February 11, 1964) is an American politician, commentator, and author who served as the ninth ___E:governor of Alaska U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Governors_of_Alaska)___ from 2006 until ___E:her resignation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Resignation_of_Sarah_Palin)___ in 2009. She was the ___E:2008 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_United_States_presidential_election)___ ___E:Republican U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican_Party_(United_States))___ ___E:vice presidential nominee U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_Republican_Party_vice_presidential_candidate_selection)___ under ___E:U.S. senator U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate)___ ___E:John McCain U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_McCain)___ .

Palin was elected to the ___E:Wasilla U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wasilla,_Alaska)___ city council in 1992 and became mayor of Wasilla in 1996. In 2003, after an unsuccessful run for ___E:lieutenant governor U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lieutenant_Governor_of_Alaska)___ , she was appointed chair of the ___E:Alaska Oil and Gas Conservation Commission U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alaska_Oil_and_Gas_Conservation_Commission)___ , responsible for overseeing the state's oil and gas fields for safety and efficiency.
In ___E:2006 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2006_Alaska_gubernatorial_election)___ , at age 42, she became the youngest person and the first woman to be elected governor of Alaska.
Immense legal fees incurred by both Palin and the state of Alaska from her fights against ethics investigations led to her resignation in 2009.
Palin was nominated as John McCain's vice presidential running mate at the ___E:2008 Republican National Convention U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_Republican_National_Convention)___ .

She was the first Republican female vice presidential nominee and the second ___E:female vice presidential U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_female_United_States_presidential_and_vice-presidential_candidates)___ nominee of a ___E:major party U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Major_party)___ , after ___E:Geraldine Ferraro U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geraldine_Ferraro)___ in ___E:1984 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1984_United_States_presidential_election)___ .

The McCain-Palin ticket subsequently lost the 2008 election to the ___E:Democratic Party U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Party_(United_States))___ 's then-U.S. senators ___E:Barack Obama U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama)___ and ___E:Joe Biden U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden)___ .
Throughout the race, her ___E:public image and experience U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_image_of_Sarah_Palin)___ came under media attention.
Although her vice presidential bid alongside McCain was unsuccessful, the 2008 presidential election significantly raised Palin's national profile.
Since her resignation as governor in 2009, she has campaigned for the fiscally conservative ___E:Tea Party movement U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tea_Party_movement)___ .

In addition, she has publicly endorsed ___E:several candidates U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mama_grizzly)___ in multiple election cycles, including ___E:Donald Trump U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump)___ in his ___E:2016 presidential campaign U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump_2016_presidential_campaign)___ .
She has also led a career as a television personality.
From 2010 to 2015, she provided political commentary for ___E:Fox News U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fox_News_Channel)___ .

She hosted ___E:TLC U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TLC_(TV_network))___ 's Sarah Palin's Alaska in 2010–11 and Amazing America with Sarah Palin on the ___E:Sportsman Channel U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sportsman_Channel)___ in 2014–15.   From 2014 to 2015, she oversaw a short-lived ___E:subscriber-based U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subscription_business_model)___ ___E:online TV channel U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/News_network)___ , the ___E:Sarah Palin Channel U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarah_Palin_Channel)___ , via ___E:TAPP TV U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TAPP_TV)___ .
Her personal memoir, Going Rogue , written following the 2008 election, sold more than one million copies.

In 2022, Palin ran in the ___E:special election U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Alaska%27s_at-large_congressional_district_special_election)___ for ___E:Alaska's at-large congressional seat U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alaska%27s_at-large_congressional_district)___ that was vacated after the death of Representative ___E:Don Young U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Young)___ ,  but lost to Democrat ___E:Mary Peltola U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Peltola)___ , who completed Young's unfinished term.  Palin faced Peltola and others again in the ___E:November general election U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_United_States_House_of_Representatives_election_in_Alaska)___ for the same seat, and again lost to Peltola, who won re-election to serve a full two-year term.

Palin was born in ___E:Sandpoint, Idaho U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sandpoint,_Idaho)___ , the third of four children (three daughters and one son) of Sarah "Sally" Heath (née Sheeran; 1940–2021),  a school secretary, and Charles R. "Chuck" Heath (born 1938), a science teacher and ___E:track-and-field U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Track-and-field)___ coach.
Palin's siblings are Chuck Jr., Heather, and Molly.
Palin is of English, Irish, and German ancestry.
When Palin was a few months old, the family moved to ___E:Skagway, Alaska U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skagway,_Alaska)___ ,  where her father had been hired to teach.

They relocated to ___E:Eagle River, Anchorage U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eagle_River,_Anchorage)___ in 1969, and settled in ___E:Wasilla, Alaska U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wasilla,_Alaska)___ , in 1972.

Palin played flute in the junior high band. She attended ___E:Wasilla High School U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wasilla_High_School)___ , where she was head of the ___E:Fellowship of Christian Athletes U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fellowship_of_Christian_Athletes)___  and a member of the girls' basketball and cross-country running teams.

During her senior year, she was co-captain and point guard of the basketball team that won the 1982 ___E:Alaska state championship U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alaska_School_Activities_Association)___ , earning the nickname "Sarah Barracuda" for her competitive streak.

In 1984, Palin won the Miss Wasilla ___E:beauty pageant U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beauty_pageant)___ ;  she finished third (as second runner-up) in the ___E:Miss Alaska U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miss_Alaska)___ pageant, where she won the title of "Miss Congeniality".
She played the flute in the talent portion of the contest.

Though one author reported that she received the Miss Congeniality award in the Miss Wasilla contest, this was disputed by another contestant and classmate of Palin's.  She received a college scholarship.
After graduating from high school in 1982, Palin enrolled at the ___E:University of Hawaii at Hilo U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Hawaii_at_Hilo)___ .

Shortly after arriving in ___E:Hawaii U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii)___ , Palin transferred to ___E:Hawaii Pacific University U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii_Pacific_University)___ in ___E:Honolulu U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honolulu)___ for a semester in the fall of 1982. She returned to the mainland, enrolling at ___E:North Idaho College U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Idaho_College)___ , a community college in ___E:Coeur d'Alene U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coeur_d%27Alene,_Idaho)___ , for the spring and fall semesters of 1983.  She transferred and enrolled at the ___E:University of Idaho U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Idaho)___ in ___E:Moscow, Idaho U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moscow,_Idaho)___ , for an academic year starting in August 1984. Beginning in the fall of 1985, she attended ___E:Matanuska-Susitna College U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matanuska-Susitna_College)___ in Alaska.

Palin returned to the University of Idaho in January 1986 and received her ___E:bachelor's degree U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor%27s_degree)___ in ___E:communications U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communication_studies)___ with an emphasis in ___E:journalism U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Journalism)___ in May 1987.

After graduation, Palin worked as a ___E:sportscaster U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_commentator)___ for ___E:KTUU-TV U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/KTUU-TV)___ and ___E:KTVA-TV U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/KTVA-TV)___ in ___E:Anchorage U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anchorage,_Alaska)___   and as a ___E:sports reporter U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_journalism)___ for the Mat-Su Valley Frontiersman ,   fulfilling an early ambition.
Palin has been a Republican since 1982.
Palin was elected to the ___E:Wasilla City Council U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayor_of_Wasilla,_Alaska)___ in 1992, winning by a margin of 530 votes to 310.

Concerned that revenue from a new Wasilla ___E:sales tax U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sales_tax)___ would not be spent wisely,  Palin ran for mayor of Wasilla in 1996, defeating incumbent mayor John Stein  by a 651–440 margin.

Her biographer described her campaign as targeting wasteful spending and high taxes;  her opponent, Stein, said that Palin introduced abortion, ___E:gun rights U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gun_politics_in_the_United_States)___ , and ___E:term limits U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Term_limits)___ as campaign issues.
The election was nonpartisan, though the state Republican Party ran advertisements for Palin.
She ran for reelection against Stein in 1999 and won, 909 votes to 292.  In 2002, she completed the second of the two consecutive three-year terms allowed by the city charter.
She was elected president of the Alaska Conference of Mayors in 1999.

Using revenue generated by a 2% sales tax, which had been approved by Wasilla voters in October 1992,   Palin cut ___E:property taxes U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Property_tax)___ by 75% and eliminated personal property and business inventory taxes.
Using ___E:municipal bonds U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Municipal_bond)___ , she made improvements to the roads and sewers and increased funding to the police department.
She oversaw creation of new bike paths and procured funding for storm-water treatment to protect freshwater resources.
At the same time, she reduced the budget of the local museum and postponed discussions about a new library and city hall, which some of the council believed was needed.
Soon after taking office in October 1996, Palin eliminated the position of museum director.
She asked for updated resumes and resignation letters from "city department heads who had been loyal to Stein", although the mayor's office was considered a non-partisan position.
These included the city police chief, public works director, finance director, and librarian.

Palin stated this request was to find out their intentions and whether they supported her. She temporarily required department heads to get her approval before talking to reporters, saying they needed to learn her administration's policies.
She created the position of city administrator  and reduced her own $68,000 salary by 10%.
By mid 1998 this action was reversed by the city council.
In October 1996, Palin asked library director Mary Ellen Emmons if she would object to the removal of a book from the library if people were picketing to have the book removed.

Emmons responded that she would, and others as well.  Palin stated that she had not been proposing censorship but had been discussing many issues with her staff that were "both rhetorical and realistic in nature."  No attempt was made to remove books from the library during Palin's tenure as mayor.

Palin said she fired Police Chief Irl Stambaugh because he did not fully support her efforts to govern the city.  Stambaugh filed a lawsuit alleging ___E:wrongful termination U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wrongful_termination)___ and violation of his free speech rights.

The judge dismissed Stambaugh's lawsuit, holding that the police chief served at the discretion of the mayor and could be terminated for nearly any reason, even a political one,   and ordered Stambaugh to pay Palin's legal fees.
During her second term as mayor, Palin proposed and promoted the construction of a municipal sports center to be financed by a 0.5%  sales tax increase and a $14.7 million bond issue.

Voters approved the measure by a 20-vote margin, and the Wasilla Multi-Use Sports Complex (later named the ___E:Curtis D. Menard Memorial Sports Center U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curtis_D._Menard_Memorial_Sports_Center)___ ) was built on time and under budget.

However, the city spent an additional $1.3 million because of an ___E:eminent domain U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eminent_domain)___ lawsuit caused by the city's failure to obtain clear title to the property before beginning construction.

The city's long-term debt grew from about $1 million to $25 million because of expenditures of $15 million for the sports complex, $5.5 million for street projects, and $3 million for water improvement projects.
The Wall Street Journal characterized the project as a "financial mess."  A city council member defended the spending increases as being necessitated by the city's growth during that time.

Palin also joined with nearby communities in hiring the ___E:Anchorage U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anchorage,_Alaska)___ -based lobbying firm of ___E:Robertson U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R._E._Robertson)___ , Monagle & Eastaugh to lobby for federal funds.

The firm secured nearly $8 million in ___E:earmarks U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earmark_(politics))___ for the Wasilla city government,  including $500,000 for a youth shelter, $1.9 million for a transportation hub, and $900,000 for sewer repairs.

In 2008, Wasilla's current mayor credited Palin's 75 percent property tax cuts and infrastructure improvements with bringing " ___E:big-box stores U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big-box_store)___ " and 50,000 shoppers per day to Wasilla.

___E:Term limits U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Term_limit)___ prevented Palin from seeking a third term in 2002. Palin ___E:endorsed U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_endorsement)___ Dianne Keller in the election to succeed her.  Keller won, defeating three opponents,  including Faye Palin (Palin's mother-in-law, the stepmother of Palin's husband).

In 2002, Palin ran for the Republican nomination for ___E:lieutenant governor U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Lieutenant_Governors_of_Alaska)___ , coming in second to ___E:Loren Leman U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loren_Leman)___ in a five-way Republican primary.

Following her defeat, she campaigned throughout the state for the nominated Republican governor-lieutenant governor ticket of ___E:Frank Murkowski U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Murkowski)___ and Leman.
Murkowski and Leman won and Murkowski resigned from his long-held ___E:U.S. Senate U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate)___ seat in December 2002 to assume the governorship.
Palin was said to be on the "short list" of possible appointees to Murkowski's U.S.

Senate seat,  but Murkowski ultimately appointed his daughter, ___E:State Representative U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alaska_House_of_Representatives)___ ___E:Lisa Murkowski U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisa_Murkowski)___ , as his successor in the Senate.

Governor Murkowski offered other jobs to Palin and, in February 2003, she accepted an appointment to the ___E:Alaska Oil and Gas Conservation Commission U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alaska_Oil_and_Gas_Conservation_Commission)___ , which oversees Alaska's oil and gas fields for safety and efficiency.
While she had little background in the area, she said she wanted to learn more about the oil industry and was named chair of the commission and ethics supervisor.

By November 2003, she was filing nonpublic ethics complaints with the state attorney general and the governor against a fellow commission member, Randy Ruedrich, a former petroleum engineer and at the time the chair of the ___E:state Republican Party U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican_Party_of_Alaska)___ .

He was forced to resign in November 2003.  Palin resigned in January 2004 and put her protests against Ruedrich's "lack of ethics" into the public arena   by filing a public complaint against Ruedrich,  who was then fined $12,000. She joined with Democratic legislator ___E:Eric Croft U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Croft)___  in complaining that ___E:Gregg Renkes U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gregg_Renkes)___ , then the ___E:attorney general of Alaska U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alaska_Attorney_General)___ ,  had a financial conflict of interest in negotiating a ___E:coal U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coal)___ exporting trade agreement.
Renkes also resigned his post.

From 2003 to June 2005, Palin served as one of three directors of " ___E:Ted Stevens U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ted_Stevens)___ Excellence in Public Service, Inc.," a ___E:527 group U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/527_group)___ designed to provide political training for Republican women in Alaska.
In 2004, Palin told the Anchorage Daily News that she had decided not to run for the U.S.

Senate that year against the Republican incumbent, ___E:Lisa Murkowski U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisa_Murkowski)___ , because her teenage son opposed it. Palin said, "How could I be the team mom if I was a U.S.
Senator?"
In 2006, running on a clean-government platform, Palin defeated incumbent Governor Frank Murkowski in the Republican gubernatorial ___E:primary U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partisan_primary)___ .
Her running mate was ___E:State Senator U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alaska_Senate)___ ___E:Sean Parnell U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Parnell)___ .

In the ___E:November election U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alaska_gubernatorial_election,_2006)___ , Palin was outspent but victorious, defeating former Democratic governor ___E:Tony Knowles U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Knowles_(politician))___ 48.3% to 41.0%.

She became Alaska's first ___E:female governor U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_female_state_governors_in_the_United_States)___ and, at the age of 42, the youngest governor in Alaskan history.

She was the state's first governor to have been born after Alaska achieved U.S. ___E:statehood U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alaska_Statehood_Act)___ , and the first who was not inaugurated in the capital, ___E:Juneau U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juneau)___ (she chose to have the ceremony in ___E:Fairbanks U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fairbanks,_Alaska)___ instead).
She took office on December 4, 2006. For most of her term, she was very popular with Alaska voters.
Polls taken in 2007 showed her with 93% and 89% popularity among all voters.

The Anchorage Daily News and The Weekly Standard called her "the most popular governor in America."   A poll taken in late September 2008, after Palin was named to the national Republican ticket, showed her popularity in Alaska at 68%.
A poll taken in May 2009 indicated Palin's popularity among Alaskans had declined to 54% positive and 41.6% negative.

Palin declared that top priorities of her administration would be resource development, education and workforce development, public health and safety, and transportation and infrastructure development.
She had championed ethics reform throughout her election campaign.

Her first legislative action after taking office was to push for a bipartisan ethics reform bill. She signed the resulting legislation in July 2007, calling it a "first step" and declaring that she remained determined to clean up Alaska politics.
Palin frequently broke with the Alaskan Republican establishment.
For example, she endorsed Parnell's bid to unseat ___E:Don Young U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Young)___ , the state's longtime ___E:at-large U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/At-large)___ U.S.
Representative.
She publicly challenged then-U.S.
Senator ___E:Ted Stevens U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ted_Stevens)___ to "come clean" about the federal investigation into his financial dealings.

She promoted the development of oil and natural-gas resources in Alaska, including drilling in the ___E:Arctic National Wildlife Refuge U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arctic_National_Wildlife_Refuge)___ (ANWR).
Proposals to drill for oil in ANWR have catalyzed ___E:national debate U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arctic_Refuge_drilling_controversy)___ .
In 2006, Palin obtained a passport.

In 2007, she traveled to ___E:Kuwait U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kuwait)___ , where she visited the Khabari Alawazem Crossing at the Kuwait–Iraq border and met with members of the ___E:Alaska National Guard U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alaska_National_Guard)___ .
On her return journey, she visited injured soldiers in Germany.
In June 2007, Palin signed a record $6.6 billion operating budget into law.  At the same time, she used her veto power to make the second-largest cuts of the capital budget in state history.
The $237 million in cuts represented over 300 local projects and reduced the capital budget to $1.6 billion.
In 2008, Palin vetoed $286 million, cutting or reducing funding for 350 projects from the ___E:FY U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fiscal_year)___ 09 capital budget.

Palin followed through on a campaign promise to sell the ___E:Westwind II U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IAI_Westwind)___ jet, a purchase made by the Murkowski administration for $2.7 million in 2005 against the wishes of the legislature.
In August 2007, the jet was listed on ___E:eBay U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EBay)___ , but the sale fell through, and the plane later sold for $2.1 million through a private brokerage firm.

Palin lived in ___E:Juneau U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juneau)___ during the legislative session, and lived in Wasilla and worked out of offices in Anchorage the rest of the year. Since the office in Anchorage was 565 miles from Juneau, while she worked there, state officials said she was permitted to claim a $58 ___E:per diem U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Per_diem)___ travel allowance and reimbursement for hotel.
She filed for per diem, claiming a total of $16,951, but rather than stay at a hotel overnight, regularly commuted the 50 miles one way to her home in Wasilla.
She did not use the former governor's private chef.
Both Republicans and Democrats criticized Palin for taking the per diem, as well as an additional $43,490 in travel expenses on occasions when her family accompanied her on state business.

Palin's staffers responded that these practices were in line with state policy, that her gubernatorial expenses were 80% below those of her predecessor Murkowski,  and that "many of the hundreds of invitations Palin receives include requests for her to bring her family, placing the definition of 'state business' with the party extending the invitation."

In February 2009, the State of Alaska, reversing a policy that had treated the payments as legitimate business expenses under the ___E:Internal Revenue Code U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internal_Revenue_Code)___ , decided that per diems paid to state employees for stays in their own homes would be treated as taxable income and will be included in employees' gross income on their ___E:W-2 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Form_W-2)___ forms.
Palin had ordered the review of the tax policy.
In December 2008, an Alaska state commission recommended increasing the governor's annual salary from $125,000 to $150,000. Palin said that she would not accept the pay raise.
In response, the commission dropped the recommendation.

In her ___E:State of the State address U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_of_the_State_address)___ on January 17, 2008, Palin declared that the people of Alaska "can and must continue to develop our economy, because we cannot and must not rely so heavily on federal government [funding]."  Alaska's federal congressional representatives cut back on ___E:pork-barrel U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pork-barrel)___ project requests during Palin's time as governor.

While the state has no sales tax or income tax, royalty revenues from the ___E:Prudhoe Bay Oil Field U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prudhoe_Bay_Oil_Field)___ (consisting mostly of state-owned lands) have supported large state budgets since 1980. The exact amounts have depended on the prevailing ___E:price of petroleum U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Price_of_petroleum)___ .

As a result, state revenues doubled to $10 billion in 2008. Despite this, for the 2009 state budget, Palin gave a list of 31 proposed federal earmarks or requests for funding, totaling $197 million, to Alaska's senior U.S. senator ___E:Ted Stevens U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ted_Stevens)___ .
This was a major decrease from earlier years.

Palin has said that her decreasing support for federal funding was a source of friction between her and the state's congressional delegation; Palin requested less in federal funding each year than her predecessor Frank Murkowski requested in his last year.

In 2002, it was proposed that a for-profit prison corporation, ___E:Cornell Corrections U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornell_Corrections)___ , build a prison on ___E:Gravina Island U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gravina_Island)___ .

To connect Gravina with nearby ___E:Ketchikan U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ketchikan)___ , on ___E:Revillagigedo Island U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Revillagigedo_Island)___ , it was originally planned that the federal government spend $175 million on building a bridge and another $75 million to connect it to the power grid with an electrical intertie.

The Ketchikan Borough Assembly turned the proposal down when the administration of Governor Tony Knowles also expressed its disfavor with the idea. Eventually, the corporation's prison plans led to the exposure of the wide-ranging ___E:Alaska political corruption probe U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alaska_political_corruption_probe)___ , which eventually ensnared Alaska's U.S. senator ___E:Ted Stevens U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ted_Stevens)___ .
The bridge idea persisted through the administration of former U.S. senator and then-governor ___E:Frank Murkowski U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Murkowski)___ .

The ___E:2005 Highway Bill U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2005_Highway_Bill)___ provided for $223m to build the ___E:Gravina Island Bridge U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gravina_Island_Bridge)___ .

The provisions and ___E:earmarks U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earmark_(politics))___  were negotiated by Alaska's Rep. ___E:Don Young U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Young)___ , who chaired the ___E:House Transportation Committee U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_House_Committee_on_Transportation_and_Infrastructure)___ , and were supported by the chair of the ___E:Senate Appropriations Committee U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Senate_Appropriations_Committee)___ , Ted Stevens.

This bridge, nicknamed "The Bridge to Nowhere" by critics, was intended to replace the ___E:auto ferry U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roll-on/roll-off)___ that is currently the only connection between Ketchikan and its airport.

While the federal earmark was withdrawn after meeting opposition from Oklahoma senator ___E:Tom Coburn U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Coburn)___ , the state of Alaska still received $300 million in transportation funding,  with which the state of Alaska continued to study improvements in access to the airport, which conceivably could include improvements to the ferry service.

In 2006, Palin had run for governor with a "build-the-bridge" plank in her platform,  saying she would "not allow the spinmeisters to turn this project ... into something that's so negative."  Palin criticized the use of the word "nowhere" as insulting to local residents   and urged speedy work on building the infrastructure "while our congressional delegation is in a strong position to assist."  Despite the demise of the bridge proposal, Palin spent $26 million in transportation funding for the planned ___E:3-mile access road U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gravina_Island_Bridge#Road_to_nowhere)___ on Gravina island that ultimately had little use.   A spokesman for ___E:Alaska's Department of Transportation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alaska_Department_of_Transportation_%26_Public_Facilities)___ said that it had been within Palin's power to cancel the road project but noted the state was considering cheaper designs to complete the bridge project, and that in any case the road would open up the surrounding lands for development.

As governor, Palin canceled the Gravina Island Bridge in September 2007, saying that Congress had "little interest in spending any more money" due to "inaccurate portrayals of the projects."  Alaska did not return the $442 million in federal transportation funds.

In 2008, as a candidate for vice president, Palin characterized her position as having told Congress "thanks, but no thanks, on that bridge to nowhere." A number of ___E:Ketchikan U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ketchikan)___ residents said that the claim was false and a betrayal of Palin's previous support for their community.
Some critics said that her statement was misleading, as she had expressed support for the spending project and kept the federal money after the project was canceled.
